summary.text: Fermat’s theorem and Legendre’s base-\(p\) digit-sum formula show that for any odd prime divisor of a composite \(n\), the product contributes more \(p\)-adic valuation than \((n-1)!\), forcing \(p\mid a(n-1)\) and hence impossibly \(p\mid2^{n-2}\); the remaining case \(n=2^m\) is excluded by an analogous exact \(2\)-adic valuation calculation. Once \(n\) is prime, Wilson’s theorem turns the assumed congruence into \(\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(2^k-1)\equiv1\pmod n\), while any proper multiplicative order \(d<n-1\) of \(2\) would make the factor \(2^d-1\) vanish and thus make that product zero.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(r)=\frac{2^{r-1}}{r!}\prod_{k=1}^{r-1}(2^k-1)\qquad(r\geq 1).
\]
We prove that, for every integer \(n>2\),
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 n\text{ is prime and }2\text{ is a primitive root modulo }n.
\]

Throughout the proof put
\[
 P_n:=\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(2^k-1).
\]
Thus the formula for the term in the hypothesis is
\[
 a(n-1)=\frac{2^{n-2}P_n}{(n-1)!}.
\]
We will first justify the required exact divisibility, and then use the identity
\[
 a(n-1)(n-1)!=2^{n-2}P_n. \tag{1}
\]

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\), and write \(s_p(x)\) for the sum of the base-\(p\) digits of \(x\). We use Legendre’s formula in its digit-sum form:
\[
 (p-1)v_p(N!)=N-s_p(N). \tag{2}
\]
This is equivalent to the usual formula \(v_p(N!)=\sum_{j\geq1}\lfloor N/p^j\rfloor\): if \(N=\sum_i d_i p^i\), multiplying that sum by \(p-1\) telescopes to \(N-\sum_i d_i\).

We also need two elementary observations about digit sums. If \(b>1\) and \(x>0\), then
\[
 s_b(x)\geq1. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, the base-\(b\) expansion of a positive number has at least one nonzero digit. More specifically, suppose that \(p\) is prime, \(p\mid n\), and \(n\) is composite. Write \(n=pk\). Necessarily \(k\geq2\), since \(k=1\) would give \(n=p\), contrary to compositeness. Now
\[
 n-1=pk-1=(p-1)+p(k-1).
\]
This is already the first step of its base-\(p\) expansion: the units digit is \(p-1\), and the remaining digits are those of \(k-1\). Since \(k-1>0\), (3) yields
\[
 s_p(n-1)=(p-1)+s_p(k-1)\geq p. \tag{4}
\]

We next obtain the divisibility needed to make (1) an identity of integers. Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Fermat’s theorem gives
\[
 2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
and hence, for every positive integer \(j\),
\[
 p\mid 2^{j(p-1)}-1. \tag{5}
\]
Set
\[
 q=\left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
The \(q\) distinct exponents
\[
 p-1,\ 2(p-1),\ldots,q(p-1)
\]
all lie between \(1\) and \(n-2\). By (5), the corresponding \(q\) factors of \(P_n\) are all divisible by \(p\). Therefore
\[
 p^q\mid P_n,
 \qquad	ext{so}\qquad
 v_p(P_n)\geq \left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{6}
\]
On the other hand, applying (2) with \(N=n-1\), and merely using \(s_p(n-1)\geq1\), gives
\[
 (p-1)v_p((n-1)!)
 =(n-1)-s_p(n-1)
 \leq n-2.
\]
Consequently
\[
 v_p((n-1)!)\leq
 \left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{7}
\]
Combining (6) and (7), every odd-prime power occurring in \((n-1)!\) occurs to at least as high an exponent in \(P_n\).

For \(p=2\), (2) and (3) similarly give
\[
 v_2((n-1)!)=(n-1)-s_2(n-1)\leq n-2.
\]
Thus the entire \(2\)-part of \((n-1)!\) divides \(2^{n-2}\). Considering every prime-power divisor of the factorial now proves
\[
 (n-1)!\mid 2^{n-2}P_n. \tag{8}
\]
Therefore the displayed formula defining \(a(n-1)\) is indeed an integer quotient and (1) follows.

We now prove that \(n\) cannot be composite under the divisibility hypothesis
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{9}
\]
There are two cases.

First suppose that the composite number \(n\) has an odd prime divisor \(p\). We sharpen (7). Since \(p\mid n\) and \(n\) is composite, (4) applies, so Legendre’s formula gives
\[
 (p-1)v_p((n-1)!)
 =(n-1)-s_p(n-1)
 \leq n-1-p.
\]
Adding \(p-1\) to both sides yields
\[
 (p-1)\bigl(v_p((n-1)!)+1\bigr)\leq n-2.
\]
Hence
\[
 v_p((n-1)!)+1
 \leq \left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor,

a nd in particular, using (6),
\[
 v_p((n-1)!)<v_p(P_n). \tag{10}
\]
(The stray spacing in “and” is immaterial; the assertion is the displayed inequality.)

Because \(p\) is odd, \(p\nmid2^{n-2}\). Taking \(p\)-adic valuations in (1) therefore gives
\[
 v_p(a(n-1))+v_p((n-1)!)=v_p(P_n).
\]
By (10), \(v_p(a(n-1))\geq1\), so
\[
 p\mid a(n-1). \tag{11}
\]
But \(p\mid n\), and (9) consequently implies
\[
 p\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
Together with (11), this says \(p\mid2^{n-2}\). A prime dividing a power of \(2\) must divide \(2\), forcing \(p=2\), contrary to the fact that \(p\) is odd. Thus a composite \(n\) satisfying (9) has no odd prime divisor.

It remains to rule out a composite number having no odd prime divisor. Such a positive integer must be a power of \(2\). For completeness, one can see this by taking \(m=v_2(n)\) and writing \(n=2^m c\). The maximality of \(m\) makes \(c\) odd. If \(c>1\), then \(c\), and hence \(n\), has a prime divisor; that prime cannot be \(2\), so it is odd, a contradiction. Hence \(c=1\) and
\[
 n=2^m.
\]
Since \(n>2\), we have \(m\geq2\).

Every factor \(2^k-1\) of \(P_n\) is odd, so
\[
 v_2(P_n)=0. \tag{12}
\]
Also
\[
 n-1=2^m-1

a nd its binary expansion consists of exactly \(m\) ones. Thus
\[
 s_2(n-1)=m.
\]
By Legendre’s formula,
\[
 v_2((n-1)!)=(n-1)-m. \tag{13}
\]
Taking \(2\)-adic valuations in (1), and using (12) and (13), gives
\[
 v_2(a(n-1))+(n-1-m)=n-2,
\]
so
\[
 v_2(a(n-1))=m-1. \tag{14}
\]

We also have \(m\leq n-2\). Indeed, for \(m\geq2\),
\[
 2^m\geq m+2,
\]
which follows by induction starting at \(m=2\); doubling the left side at the induction step more than supplies the required increment on the right. Since \(n=2^m\), this is exactly \(m\leq n-2\). Hence
\[
 2^m\mid2^{n-2}. \tag{15}
\]
On the other hand, (9) and \(n=2^m\) state that
\[
 2^m\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
Subtracting the divisible term in (15), we obtain \(2^m\mid a(n-1)\). This says \(v_2(a(n-1))\geq m\), contradicting (14). Therefore no composite \(n\) can satisfy (9), and we conclude that
\[
 n\text{ is prime}. \tag{16}
\]

It remains to prove that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo this prime \(n\). Work now modulo \(n\). Since \(n>2\), the residue class of \(2\), and hence that of \(2^{n-2}\), is nonzero and invertible. Wilson’s theorem gives
\[
 (n-1)!\equiv-1\pmod n. \tag{17}
\]
The original assumption (9) gives
\[
 a(n-1)\equiv-2^{n-2}\pmod n. \tag{18}
\]
Reduce identity (1) modulo \(n\). By (17) and (18), its left side is
\[
 a(n-1)(n-1)!
 \equiv(-2^{n-2})(-1)
 =2^{n-2}\pmod n.
\]
Its right side is \(2^{n-2}P_n\). Therefore
\[
 2^{n-2}P_n\equiv2^{n-2}\pmod n.
\]
Cancelling the nonzero class \(2^{n-2}\) gives the crucial congruence
\[
 P_n=\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(2^k-1)\equiv1\pmod n. \tag{19}
\]

Let \(d\) be the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(n\). By Fermat’s theorem, \(d\mid n-1\). If \(2\) were not a primitive root, then \(d\neq n-1\); since \(d\) is positive and divides \(n-1\), this would imply
\[
 1\leq d<n-1,
\]
so \(d\) is one of the indices \(1,2,\ldots,n-2\) occurring in \(P_n\). By the definition of multiplicative order,
\[
 2^d\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
and therefore the corresponding factor satisfies
\[
 2^d-1\equiv0\pmod n.
\]
That factor divides \(P_n\), so it would follow that \(P_n\equiv0\pmod n\), contradicting (19). Hence
\[
 d=n-1.
\]
For the prime \(n\), Euler’s totient is \(\varphi(n)=n-1\), so this says precisely that the residue class of \(2\) has order \(\varphi(n)\), i.e. that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

Combining this with (16) proves the conjecture.
